headline: Emperor Hirohito dies, a new era begins in Japan
text: Japan's Emperor Hirohito died on 7 January at the age of 87, and his son Akihito succeeds him. The new reign is called the Heisei era. The death comes while Japan's shares and land prices are soaring.

headline: George Bush sworn in as the 41st US president
text: George Bush was inaugurated on 20 January, with Dan Quayle as vice president. Ronald Reagan, who is leaving office, gave his farewell address on 11 January.

headline: Kreditanstalt puts itself under a new holding company, CS Holding
text: Early in 1989 the Kreditanstalt, called Credit Suisse abroad, turned CS Holding into a publicly traded umbrella over the bank, CS First Boston, the consultancy Fides and its stake in the utility Electrowatt. CS Holding had been set up seven years earlier mainly to hold the bank's First Boston interests. The reshuffle cost about $80 million.

headline: Siemens and GEC bid for Plessey goes to the competition watchdog
text: On 11 January the British government referred the Siemens and GEC bid for Plessey to the Monopolies and Mergers Commission, which will investigate whether it harms competition. The two companies offered 1.7 billion pounds, about $3.1 billion, in December. GEC and Plessey had already merged their telecommunications businesses in April 1988.

headline: The Boeing 747-400 enters service
text: Northwest Airlines put the Boeing 747-400 into passenger service on 9 February. It seats about 416 in three classes, and can fly 13,492 km. Northwest ordered ten of them in October 1985, and was the first airline to do so.

headline: Bush unveils a plan to rescue failed savings and loans
text: In February President Bush announced a proposal to deal with the failing savings and loan institutions, known as thrifts. A 1982 law had expanded what thrifts could lend on, letting them move into commercial property and credit lines, and many of those loans have gone bad.

headline: Schlumberger's profit rebounds
text: Schlumberger's operating results for 1988 rose to $419 million from $211 million the year before, excluding one-off items. Operating income in oilfield services tripled, as North American Wireline & Testing returned to profit. In 1988 Schlumberger raised its stake in the seismic company GECO from 50 to 75 percent.
source: https://investorcenter.slb.com/static-files/20c0ec6e-3664-4591-9972-cfee50f8ace3 (Schlumberger 1988 annual report, chairman's letter dated 7 February 1989) (read 2026-10-03)

headline: Bush attends Hirohito's funeral and visits China and South Korea
text: Between 23 and 27 February President Bush travelled to Japan for Emperor Hirohito's funeral. He then visited China and South Korea.

headline: The first GPS satellite is launched
text: The first satellite of the Global Positioning System was launched on 14 February. GPS lets a receiver on the ground work out where it is from satellite signals.

headline: Exxon Valdez spills oil in Alaska
text: The tanker Exxon Valdez ran aground on Bligh Reef in Prince William Sound, Alaska, just after midnight on 24 March, and spilled about 260,000 barrels (about 11 million gallons) of crude oil. Exxon was slow to respond: skimmers were not on hand during the first 24 hours, and a helicopter attempt to spray chemical dispersants missed its target.

headline: Buffett's letter reveals big bets on Coca-Cola and Freddie Mac
text: Berkshire Hathaway's annual letter shows that in 1988 it bought 14,172,500 Coca-Cola shares, costing $592.5 million and worth $632.4 million at year end. It also bought 2.4 million Freddie Mac preferred shares for $71.7 million. Buffett says he expects to hold both for a long time, and still holds his $700 million in Salomon.

headline: Mercedes shows its new SL roadster at Geneva
text: Mercedes-Benz unveiled its new SL sports car at the Geneva Motor Show in March. It has a roll bar that pops up automatically when needed, and the top model has a 5.0-litre V8 engine with 322 horsepower. Sales begin in the summer.

headline: Time Inc. and Warner Communications to merge
text: Time Inc. and Warner Communications announced on 4 March that they will merge, with Time Inc. buying Warner and renaming itself Time Warner. Time brings Time magazine and its publishing business, Warner brings HBO, the Warner Bros. film studio and Warner Music. Together they would be the world's largest media company.

headline: Two chemists claim 'cold fusion' in a jar
text: On 23 March chemists Stanley Pons and Martin Fleischmann announced that they had achieved nuclear fusion at room temperature, which would be a major discovery if true. Other scientists are racing to repeat the experiment and have not yet confirmed it.

headline: Intel announces the 486 chip
text: Intel announced the i486 processor on 10 April at the Comdex computer show. It is the first x86 chip with more than a million transistors, and Intel says it is about twice as fast as the 386 at the same clock speed. Samples are due in the third quarter and production quantities in the fourth.

headline: US seizes Lincoln Savings and Loan
text: On 14 April US regulators seized Lincoln Savings and Loan, owned by Charles Keating. Since 1984 it had grown five-fold, investing mainly in commercial property and shares.

headline: Hillsborough stadium crush kills 95 Liverpool fans
text: On 15 April, at an FA Cup semi-final at the Hillsborough stadium in Sheffield, a crush in an overcrowded standing area killed 95 Liverpool supporters. Britain is asking how its football grounds can be made safe.

headline: Student protests start in Beijing after Hu Yaobang's death
text: Students began gathering in Beijing on 15 April after the death of reformist leader Hu Yaobang. Their grievances include corruption and inflation, with consumer prices in Beijing up 30 percent between 1987 and 1988.

headline: Nintendo's Game Boy goes on sale in Japan
text: Nintendo released the Game Boy, a hand-held game machine, in Japan on 21 April for 12,500 yen. It has a monochrome screen and runs for up to 30 hours on four AA batteries. Super Mario Land is one of the four games sold with it, and the team that made it was led by Gunpei Yokoi.

headline: Disney-MGM Studios opens
text: Disney-MGM Studios opened at Walt Disney World on 1 May, a park that is also a working film and television studio. Only two attractions were running on the first day, the Studio Backlot Tour and The Great Movie Ride.

headline: Daimler-Benz forms the aerospace company DASA
text: Deutsche Aerospace, known as DASA, was founded on 19 May by merging Daimler-Benz's aerospace interests with MTU München and Dornier. Daimler chairman Edzard Reuter hopes it will help diversify the company beyond luxury cars and heavy trucks.

headline: Dow closes above 2,500 for the first time since the crash
text: The Dow closed above 2,500 on 19 May for the first time since Black Monday in October 1987, when it closed at 1,738.74. Before the crash it had peaked at about 2,722 in August 1987.

headline: China declares martial law as a million gather in Beijing
text: About a million people gathered in Beijing on 17 May to protest. On 20 May the State Council declared martial law and sent about 300,000 troops.

headline: Microsoft ships SQL Server and promotes Steve Ballmer
text: On 3 May Microsoft announced shipment of SQL Server 1.0, built with Ashton-Tate and Sybase, a database for office networks. The same day Steve Ballmer was promoted to senior vice president.

headline: Chinese army clears Tiananmen Square
text: Soldiers cleared Tiananmen Square on 3 and 4 June in bloody clashes. The number of dead is not known. Western nations have begun to impose arms embargoes on China.

headline: Solidarity wins Poland's first free elections
text: Poland held its first free elections on 4 June, and the Solidarity movement won overwhelmingly, a heavy blow to the communist government. A round-table agreement in April started the change.

headline: Daimler-Benz restructures into a holding company
text: Daimler-Benz is setting up Mercedes-Benz AG as a separate company for its cars and trucks. Daimler-Benz AG is to become a holding company over AEG, Mercedes-Benz and Deutsche Aerospace. Chairman Edzard Reuter wants a group that reaches beyond luxury cars and heavy trucks.

headline: Microsoft Office for the Macintosh
text: Microsoft Office for the Macintosh became available on 19 June, bundling Word 4.00, Excel 2.20, PowerPoint 2.01 and Mail 1.37. Microsoft also says sales of its mouse have passed two million.

headline: Batman opens with a $40 million weekend
text: Batman opened in American cinemas on 23 June. It took more than $40 million in its first weekend.

headline: Buffett invests $600 million in Gillette
text: Berkshire Hathaway bought $600 million of convertible preferred stock in Gillette, paying 8.75 percent and convertible after two years into about 11 percent of the company. Warren Buffett joined Gillette's board. The stake makes Gillette, which has been the target of several takeover attempts, harder for an unfriendly buyer to seize.

headline: Dow closes above 2,600
text: The Dow closed above 2,600 on 21 July. That is about a hundred points above the 2,500 mark it passed in May.

headline: United Flight 232 crashes in Sioux City
text: United Airlines Flight 232 crashed in Sioux City on 19 July. 112 people died and 184 survived.

headline: Game Boy arrives in North America
text: Nintendo's Game Boy was released in North America on 31 July. It went on sale in Japan in April.

headline: Forbes: Wal-Mart founder Sam Walton is the richest American
text: Forbes's list of billionaires, published in July, puts Sam Walton, founder of Wal-Mart, third in the world with about $8.7 billion, behind two Japanese tycoons. The top man, the railway owner Yoshiaki Tsutsumi, has at least $15 billion. The list has 55 American and 41 Japanese billionaires.

headline: Congress passes a $166 billion savings and loan bailout
text: Congress passed a $166 billion bailout law for failed savings and loans in August, and it was signed on 9 August. The law creates the Resolution Trust Corporation to take over and sell the assets of failed thrifts.

headline: Siemens and GEC raise their Plessey bid to $3.3 billion
text: In August Siemens and GEC increased their offer and made a final bid of $3.3 billion for Plessey. Their first hostile offer, in December, was worth about $3.1 billion.

headline: Dow sets its first record since the 1987 crash
text: The Dow closed at 2,734.64 on 24 August, its first record high since the crash of October 1987. Its old peak, about 2,722, was set in August 1987. Investors who held on through the crash have their money back.

headline: A human chain across the Baltic states
text: More than a quarter of all the people of the Baltic states formed a 675-kilometre human chain across the Baltic states in August. Known as the Baltic Way, it protested against Soviet occupation.

headline: Siemens and GEC complete the Plessey takeover
text: Siemens and GEC completed their takeover of Plessey on 8 September. Under their plan, outside North America GEC takes Plessey's naval systems, avionics and cryptography, while Siemens takes radar and defence systems. The telecoms venture GPT is split 60-40 between GEC and Siemens.

headline: Sony agrees to buy Columbia Pictures from Coca-Cola
text: On 27 September Sony agreed to buy Columbia Pictures Entertainment for $3.4 billion, including Coca-Cola's 49 percent stake, and to take on $1.4 billion of its debt. It is the largest Japanese purchase of an American company. Coca-Cola bought Columbia in 1982 for $692 million.

headline: Apple's first portable Macintosh
text: Apple released the Macintosh Portable on 20 September, its first battery-powered computer, at $5,799. A model with a 40 MB hard drive costs $6,400.

headline: Hurricane Hugo hits South Carolina
text: Hurricane Hugo came ashore at Sullivan's Island, South Carolina, around midnight on 21-22 September with winds of 140 mph, after 264,000 people had been told to leave the coast. It had already damaged Guadeloupe, Montserrat, Puerto Rico and the US Virgin Islands. Early estimates put the damage in the United States at about $8 billion.

headline: Baseball commissioner Bart Giamatti dies
text: Baseball commissioner A. Bartlett Giamatti died of a heart attack on 1 September, about a week after Pete Rose accepted a lifetime ban.

headline: Soviet managers graduate from McDonald's Hamburger University
text: Five managers from Moscow earned "Bachelor of Hamburgerology" degrees at McDonald's training centre in Illinois on 21 September. The first of 20 planned Moscow restaurants is due to open on 31 January 1990 near Pushkin Square, with room for 10,000 to 15,000 customers a day. Dutch experts are helping Soviet farmers grow the potatoes for the fries.

headline: 55,000 Boeing machinists go on strike
text: More than 55,000 Boeing machinists of the IAM union went on strike in early October, seeking higher pay and less mandatory overtime. Workers have been doing seven-day weeks and up to 200 hours of forced overtime every three months as Boeing tries to build more aircraft.

headline: Friday the 13th mini-crash: Dow falls 190 points
text: The Dow fell 190.58 points, or 6.91 percent, on Friday 13 October. It came four days after the Dow set a record of 2,791.41.

headline: Exxon profit falls as Valdez bills mount
text: Exxon's third-quarter profit fell 9.4 percent to $1.11 billion, because of weaker refining, marketing and chemical earnings. The company set aside $880 million in the second quarter for the Alaska oil-spill clean-up. Even so, Exxon raised its quarterly dividend by 5 cents to 60 cents per share.

headline: Loma Prieta earthquake hits San Francisco
text: A magnitude 6.9 earthquake struck the San Francisco Bay Area at 5:04 pm on 17 October, shortly before Game 3 of the World Series was due to start at Candlestick Park. A section of the Bay Bridge's upper deck fell onto the lower deck, and the upper level of Oakland's Cypress Street Viaduct collapsed onto the one below, crushing cars. President Bush signed a $1.1 billion relief package on 26 October.

headline: The Berlin Wall opens
text: On 9 November East Germany opened the Berlin Wall. It follows a year of change in Eastern Europe, with free elections in Poland in June and Hungary taking down its border fences.

headline: Mass protests begin in Czechoslovakia
text: Mass protests began in Czechoslovakia on 17 November, just over a week after the Berlin Wall opened. Dissent is spreading across Eastern Europe.

headline: Boeing strike ends
text: Boeing's machinists accepted a new contract on 22 November, ending a 48-day strike. The deal raises wages and limits forced overtime, and union leaders called it the best deal for machinists in decades.

headline: Disney releases The Little Mermaid
text: Disney's animated musical The Little Mermaid opened on 17 November. Last year Disney's Who Framed Roger Rabbit was the second-highest-grossing film of 1988.

headline: Bush and Gorbachev meet off Malta
text: President Bush and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev held a summit off Malta on 3 December. It comes after the Berlin Wall opened on 9 November.

headline: Romania's dictator Ceausescu is executed
text: After an uprising that began in Timisoara on 16 December and reached Bucharest on 21 December, Romanian dictator Nicolae Ceausescu fled and was executed on 25 December. Unlike elsewhere in the region, Romania's revolution has been violent.

headline: IBM to cut 10,000 US jobs
text: IBM announced in early December that it will cut 10,000 US jobs through retirement and separation incentives, not layoffs. It is setting aside $2.3 billion for the cuts and will buy back $4 billion of its own shares. IBM blames slow growth in its home market, while business is stronger in Europe and Asia.

headline: Nikkei ends the decade at a record 38,915.87
text: Tokyo's Nikkei 225 closed at 38,915.87 on 29 December, a record. The index has grown sixfold during the 1980s.

headline: The Industrial Bank of Japan ranks among the world's most valuable companies
text: By some counts the Industrial Bank of Japan is now among the most valuable companies in the world, worth about $104 billion on the stock market, well ahead of Exxon at about $64 billion. Japanese banks such as Sumitomo, Fuji and Dai-Ichi Kangyo also rank near the top, lifted by Tokyo's booming share prices.

headline: Daimler-Benz takes over MBB
text: Daimler-Benz acquired the aerospace group Messerschmitt-Bölkow-Blohm in December and merged it into DASA. The Federal Cartel Office had opposed the deal, but in September Economics Minister Helmut Haussmann overruled it and approved the takeover with conditions.

headline: Microsoft's president Jon Shirley to retire
text: Microsoft announced on 27 December that Jon Shirley will retire as president and chief operating officer on 30 June 1990. In its 1989 financial year Microsoft's sales reached $804.5 million, with 4,037 employees.

headline: Dow ends 1989 at 2,753.20
text: The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed 1989 at 2,753.20, up 26.96 percent on the year, and above the record set before the October 1987 crash. A year ago it gained 11.85 percent.
